item.title: Verifying a download
item.description:
Each release of authnd, authn-bridge, authn-revokd and sshcert publishes six static binaries (CGO_ENABLED=0: linux, darwin and windows, on amd64 and arm64), a SHA256SUMS file, and a build-provenance attestation for every binary. The examples below use authn-bridge v0.23.4; the other programs work the same way with their own repository and name.

gh release download v0.23.4 --repo go-authn/bridge

1. The checksum 

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing # macOS: shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
authn-bridge-darwin-amd64: OK
authn-bridge-darwin-arm64: OK
authn-bridge-linux-amd64: OK
authn-bridge-linux-arm64: OK
authn-bridge-windows-amd64.exe: OK
authn-bridge-windows-arm64.exe: OK

This proves the file is the one the release lists, and nothing more: whoever could replace a binary on the release page could replace SHA256SUMS beside it.

2. The provenance 

gh attestation verify authn-bridge-linux-amd64 --repo go-authn/bridge
echo $?

The attestation is signed by GitHub for the workflow run that built the file,so it names the repository and the workflow, not a key somebody holds.

Read the exit status, not the output. Without a terminal, some versions ofgh print nothing at all when the verification succeeds: measured with gh 2.65.0 on authnd, a genuine binary gave exit status 0 and an empty output. A binary with one byte appended gave exit status 1 andError: failed to fetch attestations from go-authn/authnd: HTTP 404: Not Found,because no attestation exists for its digest. Silence is not the failure; a non-zero status is.

3. What the binary says about itself 

go version -m authn-bridge-linux-amd64
authn-bridge-linux-amd64: go1.27.3
path github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge
mod github.com/go-authn/bridge v0.23.4
build -trimpath=true
build CGO_ENABLED=0
build vcs.revision=6e0156cb516ace9091d4070c425258febc48f6ee
build vcs.modified=false

(lines shortened to the ones that matter; the first names the Go toolchain that built the binary). The mod line must be the tag exactly, and vcs.modified must be false: a build from a tree with uncommitted changes says true, and its version reads v0.23.4+dirty. The release workflow refuses to publish unless every one of the six binaries passes both checks, and unless the program prints the tag as the last word of its version line:

$ authnd --version
authnd version v0.12.4
$ authn-bridge --version
authn-bridge version v0.23.4
$ authn-revokd -version
authn-revokd v0.6.6

Release binaries are linked with -ldflags="-w" (authnd from v0.12.2, authn-bridge from v0.23.4, authn-revokd from v0.6.6, sshcert from v0.1.8), not -s -w: the debug information is omitted and the symbol table is kept. Without the symbol table, govulncheck -mode binary cannot tell which functions are present, falls back to module level and reports vulnerabilities in code that is not linked; with it, the scan is precise. The binaries are 7 to 10 % larger.

authnd and authn-bridge take --version; authn-revokd takes -version, Go’s standard flag syntax. From v0.6.1 it prints on standard output, like the other two, so v=$(authn-revokd -version) captures it.

Which releases have binaries

Binaries, sums and attestations are published from authnd v0.9.2, authn-bridge v0.19.3, authn-revokd v0.5.0 and sshcert v0.1.2. The first release of each built its binaries inside the checkout and reported +dirty; that was fixed in the next one, and the per-binary check came after that. Earlier tags are source-only: build them with go install …@<tag>, which records the tag in the build information that go version -m reads. What the program prints is not always that: sshcert-authorize printed dev for a go install build until v0.1.5, and revokd has no -version before v0.5.0.

item.title: How a list is verified
item.description:
A list that does not verify is never written, served or used. The last good copy stays. A fetch that fails, for any reason, never replaces it with an empty answer, which would revoke nothing.

The signature

A KRL is fetched with its signature, <url>.sig: an armored SSHSIG over the whole file, by the SSH CA key configured as ssh_ca, in the namespacekrl@go-authn.github.io. The namespace keeps the signature from being taken for anything else. A signer hashes with SHA-512; SHA-256 is accepted too. An RSA signature in the SHA-1 form, which PROTOCOL.sshsig forbids, is refused.

The KRL itself must parse as sshd parses it, and must not carry OpenSSH’s own signature section, which OpenSSH never verifies.

A list signed by any other key is refused:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd-other.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: revocation: the KRL's signature does not verify by SHA256:6iM7YPhdfXxQEj/PUf7CYbqBuSiVTVMx2VADj63cAg4: public key does not match
bridge-x509: version 1793014030593, issued 2026-10-26T11:27:10Z, expires 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z
output sshd: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/other.krl
output tls: wrote /tmp/authn/revokd/out/other.crl
authn-revokd: not current: bridge-ssh

Here ssh_ca named a key that did not sign bridge’s list, and the error names that key. A signature that does not verify may also be a list issued again between the two requests, so both are fetched once more before it is reported.This was the first fetch of that source, so there was no good copy to keep, and the output is the fail-closed list at once. (Before v0.6.2 the same failure carried “the list changed between it and its signature” in front of the message above, as if the list had been issued again.)

The signature is fetched with If-Match: <the list's ETag>. A list issued again between the two requests answers 412, and both are fetched again.

A CRL is checked against the CA certificate configured as x509_ca: its signature first, on the raw bytes, before the rest is parsed, so a large CRL signed by anybody costs a signature check rather than a parse. Then its issuer must be that certificate’s subject; it must have a CRL Number and anextUpdate after its thisUpdate; and it must not be a delta CRL, nor carry a critical extension other than the CRL Number and the Authority Key Identifier,nor a critical entry extension.

A KRL must also say when it expires, in the expires@go-authn.github.io extension: one that does not could never be told from a stale one.

Bodies are bounded: a KRL at 32 MiB, its signature at 64 KiB, a CRL at 64 MiB.

The dates

A list is current when:

  • now is before its expiry (the KRL’s extension, the CRL’s nextUpdate);
  • it was not issued more than five minutes in the future: an issuer whose clock is ahead by more than that writes lists whose age cannot be known;
  • with max_age, it was issued no longer ago than that.

A list that is not current is refused when fetched. A 304 Not Modified is no news: the copy held may have expired since, and it is judged again at every sync.

Never older than the list held

A list’s position is its version (the KRL’s krl_version, the CRL Number), then its issue time (the KRL’s generation date, the CRL’sthisUpdate). A list may replace the one held only when it has a higher version, or the same version issued later: the same revocations, issued again with a new expiry. Anything else is a rollback: a replayed or restored older list, still signed and unexpired, that would un-revoke what the newer one revoked.

Across restarts too

The list held is kept in state_dir, one file per source holding the list and its signature together, written by a single rename with the directory synced.At start each copy is verified again (expired or not, it orders what comes next), and a copy that no longer verifies is not trusted, not even to order the next one, and is said so in the log.

Here a source is pointed, after a restart, at a list an earlier bridge process served nineteen seconds before, still signed and still unexpired:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: version 0, issued 2026-10-26T11:27:10Z, expires 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z
bridge-x509: version 1793014030593, issued 2026-10-26T11:27:10Z, expires 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z
$ authn-revokd -config revokd-old.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: file:///tmp/authn/revokd/old/bridge.krl: revocation: the list is older than the one held: version 0 issued at 2026-10-26T11:26:49Z, the copy held at 2026-10-26T11:27:10Z
authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z)
$ ssh-keygen -Q -l -f out/sshd.krl
# KRL version 0
# Generated at 20261026T122710
# Comment: authn-revokd sshd

The first run wrote no output: the files already held those lists. The older list is refused and the output keeps the newer one. The process that refused it had never seen the newer list: it read it back from state_dir.

Since the state is what makes a rollback detectable, the directory is held to sshd’s StrictModes rule (the configuration).A crash between two writes cannot leave a pair that fails to verify, which would take the rollback guard with it: the list and its signature are one file.

What -once reports

-once exits 1 when a source has no current list, when its last fetch failed, or when an output could not be written, and its last line says which of the first two it is:

last line the source its outputs
not current: <source> holds no current list: never fetched, expired, or past max_age failed closed for sshd
not fetched: <source> (the list held is current until <T>) its fetch failed, but the copy held is still current written from that copy, unchanged, until T

Here the issuer is stopped while both lists held are still current:

$ authn-revokd -config revokd.hcl -once
bridge-ssh: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/krl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
bridge-x509: revocation: Get "http://127.0.0.1:28473/x509/crl": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:28473: connect: connection refused
authn-revokd: not fetched: bridge-ssh (the list held is current until 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z), bridge-x509 (the list held is current until 2026-10-26T12:27:10Z)

That run left sshd.krl as it was. Once a list held lapses, the same source is reported not current, and both kinds can share the line, as onwhen a list lapses. Before v0.6.2 both cases were reported not current, which said a list had lapsed when only its fetch had failed; the exit status was 1 then too.

The mirror’s /healthz judges by the copy held instead, and answered ok while the issuer was down and the copies still current.

item.title: Security
item.description:
go-authn is asked to prove people, so its refusals are the design rather than the exceptions. This section gathers the ones that cross program boundaries;each program’s own pages say what it refuses on its own.

The refusals that matter most

what is refused why
authnd a search by anyone but a declared reader a bind proves who somebody is; it is not permission to list everybody
authnd a Kerberos ticket for a person whose source holds no password a KDC needs a key derived from the password; an NT hash or a password check cannot produce one (why)
authnd a kerberos block beside an mfa block a kinit carries the password and nothing else, so the realm would issue tickets on one factor to people the mfa block says need two
authn-bridge an assertion nobody signed, an identifier from outside the institution’s own scope every member of a federation is trusted, so each must be held to its own people: otherwise any one institution could name anybody
authn-revokd a list that is unsigned, expired, or older than the one it holds a mirror in between may delay a list, never forge it or roll it back
authn-revokd trusting a list that has lapsed it writes one that revokes the CA itself, so sshd refuses rather than trusting a stale list
sshcert-authorize a certificate whose domain grant does not name this host a certificate from a federation CA is not, by itself, permission for every host that trusts that CA

A revocation, end to end

  1. authn-bridge signs and dates a KRL (for SSH certificates) and a CRL (for X.509 client certificates), and publishes them.
  2. authn-revokd fetches each list,verifies its signature and dates, refuses one older than the list it holds(across a restart too), and only then writes it where the server reads it.
  3. sshd (RevokedKeys), go-fileshare and anything else read a file that has already been verified.

A CAEP session-revoked event, through the provider’s Shared Signals transmitter, voids what no list can name: everything issued to a person before a given moment. go-fileshare’s documentation describes the receiving side:revocation lists,shared signals.

Releases

Every binary is built by the release workflow from a tagged commit and can be checked three ways: verifying a download.
